notes: Ordinance "Done at Charleston the twentieth day of December" 1860; no referendum. Senators left before the ordinance: Chesnut withdrew 1860-11-10 (the first senator to go), Hammond 1860-11-11. The four representatives retired 1860-12-21 and their withdrawal letter was received by the House 1860-12-24 — the date used here as the last departure event. Chesnut's seat was not formally vacated until the Senate expelled him 1861-07-11. Readmission act passed over President Johnson's veto 1868-06-25 and was conditional on the state legislature ratifying the Fourteenth Amendment; senators seated 1868-07-15 and 1868-07-16, representatives from 1868-07-18.

Ordinance "ordained and declared in convention the 9th day of January" 1861; no referendum. Rep. L. Q. C. Lamar left 1860-12-20; four other representatives withdrew 1861-01-12; Sen. Albert G. Brown withdrew 1861-01-12; Sen. Jefferson Davis withdrew 1861-01-21 (the last of the delegation). Both Senate seats were declared vacant by Senate resolution 1861-03-14. On readmission, Senators Ames and Revels and five representatives were all seated 1870-02-23, the day the act was approved; Revels took the oath 1870-02-25.

Ordinance "Passed 10 Jan 1861"; no referendum. Whole delegation left the same day: Senators Yulee and Mallory and the state's single representative, George S. Hawkins, all withdrew 1861-01-21. Mallory's seat was declared vacant 1861-03-14; Yulee's term expired 1861-03-03 and the Senate took no formal action against him. Sen. Osborn seated 1868-06-25 and Rep. C. M. Hamilton 1868-07-01. Caution: the 40th-Congress roster lists Sen. Adonijah Welch "from June 17, 1868," which precedes the readmission act — probably a credentials or election date rather than a seating date.

Ordinance "Done ... at Montgomery, on this, the eleventh day of January" 1861; no referendum. Six representatives withdrew 1861-01-21; Rep. Williamson R. W. Cobb withdrew 1861-01-30, the last member of the delegation to go. SOURCES DISAGREE on Sen. Benjamin Fitzpatrick: the 36th-Congress record has him withdrawing 1861-01-21, while the Senate Historical Office records his salary paid to 1861-02-04 and his term expiring 1861-03-03 with no Senate action taken. Sen. Clement Clay did not appear 1861-03-14 and his seat was declared vacant that day. Senators seated 1868-07-13, representatives from 1868-07-21.

readmission_basis: Act of Congress, 16 Stat. 363 (ch. CCXCIX) — second readmission
notes: READMITTED TWICE — this row records the second and final readmission. The Act of 1868-06-25 (15 Stat. 73) admitted Georgia on extra conditions; its representatives were seated 1868-07-25 but its senators never were. In September 1868 the reconstructed legislature expelled all but two of its thirty-three Black members; in December 1869 Congress returned Georgia to military rule — the only state so treated twice — and Gen. Alfred Terry reinstated the Black legislators in early 1870. The Act of 1870-07-15, "An Act relating to the State of Georgia," then declared Georgia "entitled to representation." Representatives were seated 1870-12-22 and the senators only on 1871-02-01 (Hill) and 1871-02-24 (Miller), so full representation in both chambers did not resume until February 1871. SECESSION DATE ALSO CONTESTED: the convention at Milledgeville voted 208-89 on 1861-01-19 and its president proclaimed Georgia seceded that afternoon (used here); 293 delegates signed the engrossed ordinance 1861-01-21; the ordinance is sometimes given as effective 1861-01-22; and the Wikipedia 36th-Congress timeline says 1861-01-18, which no other source supports and which is treated here as an error. Representation lost: representatives withdrew 1861-01-23, Sen. Iverson 1861-01-28, Sen. Toombs 1861-02-04 (last to go; seat declared vacant 1861-03-14).

Ordinance "Adopted in convention at Baton Rouge this 26th day of January, 1861"; no referendum. Senators Benjamin and Slidell withdrew 1861-02-04 (Benjamin's seat declared vacant 1861-03-14; Slidell's term expired 1861-03-03). Rep. Miles Taylor submitted the ordinance to the Clerk and withdrew 1861-02-05, the date used here. Rep. John E. Bouligny never withdrew and sat until the 36th Congress expired 1861-03-03, so on a strict "last member seated" reading Louisiana's date is 1861-03-03. Senators seated 1868-07-08 and 1868-07-09, representatives from 1868-07-18.

THREE DEFENSIBLE DATES. The convention at Austin adopted the ordinance 1861-02-01 (used here); by its own sec. 2 it was submitted to the voters and ratified 1861-02-23, 46,153 to 14,747; and it provided that it "shall take effect and be in force on and after the 2d day of March, A.D. 1861." Sen. Wigfall withdrew 1861-03-23, the last Texan seated; Sen. Hemphill simply did not appear 1861-03-04; both were expelled 1861-07-11. Sen. Flanagan and three representatives were seated 1870-03-30, the day the act was approved; Sen. M. C. Hamilton and the remaining representatives 1870-03-31.

THREE DEFENSIBLE DATES, all attested by two independent sources. (1) 1861-04-04: the convention, sitting at Richmond since 1861-02-13, voted down secession 90 to 45. (2) 1861-04-17: after Fort Sumter and Lincoln's call for volunteers, the convention adopted the Ordinance of Secession 88 to 55 — used here as the adoption date. (3) 1861-05-23: the ordinance, by its own terms effective only "when ratified by a majority of the voters," was ratified 132,201 to 37,451. A defensible alternative for a strict legal-effect rule is 1861-05-23. REPRESENTATION LOST PRECEDES SECESSION: Senators Mason and Hunter withdrew 1861-03-28, three weeks before the ordinance, and were expelled 1861-07-11. But Virginia was never actually unrepresented — the pro-Union Restored Government's senators Willey and Carlile were seated 1861-07-09 and five Virginia representatives sat in the 37th Congress, so any denominator rule that drops Virginia between 1861 and 1870 should be flagged. Senators Lewis and Johnston and most representatives seated 1870-01-26, the day the act was approved.

Ordinance "Adopted and passed in open convention on the 6th day of May, A.D. 1861"; no referendum. Arkansas seceded after the 36th Congress expired 1861-03-03, so its representatives simply served out their terms and none were elected to the 37th. Neither Sen. Sebastian nor Sen. Mitchel ever formally notified the Senate of withdrawal; the Senate Historical Office records only their expulsion 1861-07-11, used here. An alternative is 1861-03-28, the adjournment of the special Senate session after which neither senator appeared (inferred from the Senate chronology, not stated as such by any source). Sebastian's expulsion was posthumously annulled by the Senate in 1877. Readmission act passed over veto 1868-06-22; Sen. McDonald and two representatives seated the same day.

Ordinance "Done in convention at the city of Raleigh, this the 20th day of May" 1861; no referendum. REPRESENTATION LOST MORE THAN TWO MONTHS BEFORE SECESSION: Sen. Bragg withdrew 1861-03-08 and Sen. Clingman 1861-03-11 (used here); both were expelled 1861-07-11, which is the alternative date if the formal vacating of the seats is what matters. North Carolina's representatives' terms expired with the 36th Congress 1861-03-03 and none were elected to the 37th. Senators seated 1868-07-14, representatives from 1868-07-15.

secession_basis: legislative Declaration of Independence and Ordinance, ratified by referendum
readmission_basis: Joint Resolution of Congress, 14 Stat. 364 (Res. No. 73)
notes: NO CONVENTION — the only one of the eleven. A referendum on 1861-02-09 rejected calling a secession convention. The General Assembly instead adopted a "Declaration of Independence and Ordinance" on 1861-05-06 and sent it to the voters, who approved it 1861-06-08 by 104,471 to 47,183. SOURCES DISAGREE: the Senate Historical Office dates Tennessee's secession to 1861-06-08 ("the last state to secede"), the American Battlefield Trust and Wikipedia to 1861-05-06 for the instrument with the 1861-06-08 ratification noted; 1861-05-06 is used here for parallelism with the other ten adoption dates. TENNESSEE WAS NEVER WHOLLY UNREPRESENTED: Sen. Nicholson withdrew 1861-03-03 (used here) and was expelled 1861-07-11, but Sen. Andrew Johnson kept his seat until 1862-03-04, and three Tennessee representatives sat in the 37th Congress. First state restored, and the only one restored before the Reconstruction Acts: seven representatives and Sen. Fowler seated 1866-07-24, Sen. Patterson 1866-07-28.
